title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
Criminals are using AI-generated deepfakes to impersonate real people, including immigration attorneys in South Florida, and trick victims into sending money. The technology enables voice cloning from social media, spoofed phone numbers, and fabricated images that make fraud schemes more convincing. The scams have targeted immigrants seeking legal services and families with access to cryptocurrency, resulting in reported losses in the hundreds of thousands of dollars.

This is impersonation enabled by deployed AI systems that generate synthetic media. The failure occurred at the point where victims could not distinguish synthetic voices and images from authentic ones. Detection would have required either stronger verification protocols on the victim's end (calling known numbers to confirm requests) or technical measures that make deepfakes harder to create or distribute, but it is not established what technical safeguards existed in the systems used to distribute these frauds.

It is not established whether the AI systems used to create these deepfakes were built by the scammers themselves, purchased as commercial products, or accessed through other means.

summary:
Criminals are increasingly using artificial intelligence to create convincing deepfakes for scamming people out of money. The FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report shows Americans lost nearly $893 million to AI-enabled scams last year. Recent cases in Georgia and South Florida demonstrate this trend, including an $800,000 cryptocurrency scam targeting a Cobb County couple and a scheme where scammers cloned a South Florida immigration attorney's voice to target immigrants. The technology allows fraudsters to clone voices from social media, spoof phone numbers, create fake photographs, and research personal relationships to make their schemes more believable.

Florida reported 350 AI-related complaints with nearly $39.9 million in losses, while Georgia had 71 complaints totaling over $10.4 million. Experts warn these numbers likely undercount actual losses since many victims never report scams. To protect themselves, people should establish code words with family members, verify urgent requests by calling known numbers directly, and avoid sending money based on phone calls alone. Banks and law enforcement urge consumers to pause before responding to unexpected requests and contact financial institutions immediately if targeted.
